chosen_title: Two 'Super-Puff' Planets Lighter Than Cotton Candy Discovered by Researchers
source: Good News Network / CBC / NASA TESS Mission
caption:
Two new planets are 1,000 times Earth's size. That's not the bizarre part. 🪐

Researchers using NASA's TESS mission have discovered two so-called 'super-puff' exoplanets that are roughly 1,000 times larger than Earth by volume — yet so incredibly low in density that their material is lighter than cotton candy. That means these giants, despite their colossal size, have almost no mass to speak of.

Super-puff planets are one of astronomy's most puzzling categories. Scientists believe they have a small rocky or icy core surrounded by a vast, extended atmosphere — so thin and spread out that the planet's average density barely registers. What makes this discovery unusual is finding two of them together, giving researchers a rare pair to study side by side.

The catch: scientists aren't sure how super-puffs survive. Their wispy atmospheres should be slowly boiling away from stellar radiation — meaning these worlds may be temporary by cosmic standards.

Why it matters: every planet like this forces us to rethink what a 'planet' can be — and sharpens our models of how our own solar system came to look the way it does.

slides.label: THE STORY
slides.headline: Meet the two impossible planets
slides.body: Researchers using NASA's TESS planet-hunting mission have confirmed two 'super-puff' exoplanets, each approximately 1,000 times larger than Earth by volume. The twist: despite their enormous size, both planets have such extraordinarily low density that their material is lighter than cotton candy. They belong to a rare and poorly understood class of worlds that challenge everything we know about how planets form and hold themselves together.

slides.label: THE NUMBER
slides.caption: Each super-puff planet is roughly 1,000 times larger than Earth in volume — yet so feather-light in density that the average material across the whole planet is less dense than the spun sugar in a carnival cotton candy cone.

slides.label: HOW IT WORKS
slides.art_prompt: A cutaway cartoon diagram of a super-puff planet: a vast, translucent cotton-candy-pink sphere dominates the frame, its interior showing a tiny dense pebble-sized rocky core at the very center, surrounded by an enormous billowing atmosphere hundreds of times the core's size — like a marble inside a hot-air balloon the size of a house. A tiny blue Earth floats beside it for scale, barely visible. Stars pepper the cosmic background.
slides.headline: Mostly atmosphere — almost no substance
slides.body: Scientists believe super-puff planets have a small rocky or icy core wrapped in a hugely extended, gossamer-thin atmosphere. That atmosphere is so vast and spread out that when you average the density across the whole planet, the number almost vanishes — producing a world that is physically enormous but nearly weightless.

slides.label: WHY IT MATTERS
points: Super-puff planets are one of astronomy's most contested mysteries — scientists still debate whether their bloated atmospheres can survive long-term without being slowly baked away by their host star's radiation.
Finding two super-puffs at once gives researchers a rare side-by-side comparison, making it far easier to study how these extreme worlds form, evolve, and manage to stay intact.
NASA's TESS mission was designed to find Earth-like worlds, but keeps delivering rule-breaking planets like these — dramatically widening what scientists consider physically possible.
Every strange planet discovered sharpens the models scientists use to understand our own solar system's four-billion-year history, including why Earth turned out the way it did.
